slides: Open by framing the exponential map as the chapter's bridge from linear infinitesimal data to nonlinear group geometry. The lecture will keep returning to the same question: what does a tangent vector at the identity produce after we let it flow for time one?

Use SO(2) as the clean first model. The skew generator A gives a left-invariant flow, its integral curve through the identity is gamma_A(t) = exp(tA), and addition of times becomes multiplication of group elements. The notebook check verifies the group law, inverse, and determinant numerically.

This slide turns the matrix exponential into an ODE solver. For a constant matrix A, exp(tA) is the flow of the left-invariant equation gamma prime equals gamma A. Rotation, shear, and anisotropic scaling look different, but the symbolic residual check says all three solve the same structural equation.

Define the exponential map by starting with X in the Lie algebra, following the unique one-parameter subgroup generated by X, and evaluating at time one. Emphasize the local theorem: the derivative at zero is the identity, so exponential coordinates give a genuine chart near the identity even though the group may be curved.

Pause on the difference between local coordinates and global topology. The map from R to S^1 has nonzero derivative at zero and is locally a coordinate, but theta and theta plus 2 pi land on the same group element. This is the warning students should remember whenever they try to invert exp globally.

Present the closed subgroup theorem through the slice picture. The Lie algebra h consists of directions whose whole one-parameter subgroup remains in H. After choosing a complement b, exponential coordinates separate the subgroup directions from transverse directions near the identity.

Translate a Lie group action into vector fields on the acted-on manifold. For the standard rotation action, differentiating the orbit through (x,y) gives the field (-y,x), tangent to circles. The finite-difference check at the marked point agrees with the infinitesimal generator.

Now zoom out to the classification result. Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra integrates to a simply connected Lie group, and other connected groups with that algebra are quotients by discrete normal subgroups. The R to R/Z example is the same wrapping phenomenon from the exponential slide seen as a quotient.

Finish the algebra-to-group dictionary with normality. Connected normal subgroups correspond to ideals, and the adjoint representation is the translator. In the two-dimensional example, [H,E] = 2E keeps span(E) stable, and conjugation by exp(tH) only rescales that same line.

Close by collecting the operating rules. Lines in the algebra become one-parameter subgroups, exp is locally a chart but globally can wrap, closed subgroups are detected by exponential slices, actions differentiate to vector fields, and normal connected subgroups are recognized as ideals.
